title: ‘Sinking’ African megacities will expose seven million people to flooding by 2050 - Carbon Brief
gist: A Science Advances study combining 4,000+ satellite images with IPCC sea level projections finds subsidence plus sea level rise could expose over seven million people, one million buildings and $180bn of assets in 20 African coastal megacities to flooding by 2050. Lagos and Alexandria, sinking 5.2-6.3mm a year, account for five million people and $150bn of that exposure; estimates are worst-case (no defences, 2020 population).

insights.so_what: Sizes a large, under-monitored climate-risk pool for African coastal real estate, infrastructure and insurers.

insights.claim: Lagos (Nigeria) and Alexandria (Egypt) are the most flood-vulnerable African megacities, together accounting for about five million exposed people and $150bn of exposed assets by mid-century, roughly 83% of the study's total asset exposure.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Concentrated risk: adaptation finance, sovereign climate risk and property exposure in Nigeria and Egypt deserve the closest watch.

insights.claim: Djibouti City, Mogadishu and Tripoli face minimal economic flood exposure because of their smaller populations and infrastructure bases, despite being coastal.

insights.so_what: Exposure is driven by asset density, not just geography; risk screens should weight population and infrastructure base.

themes.theme: Subsidence as a hidden flood multiplier

insights.claim: Human activity such as groundwater pumping and fossil fuel drilling causes land subsidence, and this vertical land movement can amplify the effective sea level rise faced by coastal cities.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Extraction-driven subsidence is a local, controllable driver of flood risk that pure sea-level models miss.
insights.locator: Human activity, such as pumping groundwater

insights.claim: Satellite analysis identifies Lagos and Alexandria as subsidence hotspots sinking at 5.2mm and 6.3mm per year respectively, rates comparable to Jakarta, Manila and Ho Chi Minh City, which have some of the highest subsidence rates observed.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Puts African megacities in the same risk class as south-east Asia's sinking cities, a useful analogue for adaptation costs.

insights.claim: The study combined more than 4,000 satellite images of Africa's coastline with IPCC sixth assessment report sea level projections under three emissions scenarios, plus 2020 population, building footprint and GDP-per-capita data, to estimate city flood exposure through the 21st century.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: A replicable satellite-plus-IPCC exposure framework that can be applied to other coastal markets.
insights.locator: The researchers combined more than 4,000 satellite images

insights.claim: Because the model holds population at 2020 levels and assumes no coastal defences, its African flood-exposure estimates are a worst-case physical picture that could be too high if people relocate or too low if urban growth continues.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Treat the headline figures as directional: defences lower them, rapid urbanisation raises them.
insights.quote: the flood model assumes no coastal defenses, so the estimates are a worst-case physical picture

insights.claim: Africa is the world's fastest-urbanising region, with cities growing about 3.5% a year, which suggests static-population flood-exposure estimates likely understate future risk (the article also states Africa's urban population is expected to double to 1.4bn by 2050, though its quoted starting figure of 7m appears inconsistent).
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Rapid urban growth into exposed coastal zones compounds flood risk and adaptation demand over time.
insights.locator: Africa is the world’s fastest-urbanising region

insights.claim: Subsidence in African coastal cities has not been consistently monitored due to a lack of local data, and the authors say their satellite method could be applied to other data-scarce coastal regions across the global south.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Satellite-based subsidence monitoring is an emerging data/service opportunity for climate-risk analytics in data-poor markets.
